A: did u see Darshan's voice note

A: hes such a clown

Urmila typed "stop" and deleted it. Typed "this isn't funny" and deleted that too.

Private message
Urmila: hey. i saw the chat. its not ok
Urmila: do you want to talk?
Darshan: i left the group
Urmila: good. i'm here. i can come with you to tell our class teacher tomorrow if you want
Darshan: ok
Darshan: thanks for messaging me

qa.q: What did Urmila write privately to Darshan?
qa.a: Urmila wrote "i saw the chat. its not ok" and asked, "do you want to talk?"

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling when she typed and deleted her messages in the group chat?
qa.a: Urmila seemed uneasy and unsure; typing and deleting twice suggests a wish to speak up, perhaps held back by fear of the group turning on Urmila.

qa.q: What options did Urmila have, and which did Urmila choose?
qa.a: Urmila could join in, stay silent or defend Darshan publicly; Urmila chose to message Darshan privately and offered to go to the teacher with him.

qa.q: How might Darshan have felt when he saw Urmila's message?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved not to be alone after being laughed at, and his short replies show how much it mattered.

grounding: A teen sees a pile-on against one classmate and, rather than join or stay silent, messages the target privately.

passage: The video went up at 8 p.m.: Avni singing on the Ganesh festival stage in their small town, her voice cracking on the high note. By nine the class group had eighty messages. Crying-laughing faces. "Donkey solo." Someone turned it into a sticker. Farhan's thumb hovered. One laughing face and he'd fit in. Staying quiet was easier still. He remembered Avni lending him her notes when he had typhoid. He typed in the group, "Guys, enough. She was brave to get on stage." Two people replied with eye-rolls. Then he opened a private chat. "Hey, I saw the group. That's not ok. You ok?" Avni replied after a long minute: "thanks. I thought everyone was laughing." Farhan showed the group to his mother, who messaged the class teacher that night; by morning the sticker was gone.

qa.q: When did the video go up?
qa.a: The video went up at 8 p.m.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling as his thumb hovered?
qa.a: Farhan felt torn and uneasy, tempted to fit in by laughing but remembering Avni's kindness with the notes.

qa.q: Which choices did Farhan make, and why do they matter?
qa.a: He spoke up once in the group, messaged Avni privately and showed his mother, so Avni knew someone was with her and an adult could step in.

qa.q: How might Avni feel reading Farhan's private message?
qa.a: Avni likely feels a little less alone and relieved, since she thought everyone was laughing.

grounding: Illustrates a teen watching a group-chat pile-on, choosing to defend the target and message her privately rather than join or stay silent.

passage: In Chicago, the basketball team chat blew up after Jamal missed the final free throw. "Choke artist." "Brick Jamal." Somebody posted a slowed-down clip with sad music. Javier lay on his bed reading it, stomach tight. He wasn't brave enough to take on the whole team in public; the captain had started it. But he opened a private message. "Hey man. The chat is out of line. You carried us in the third quarter. Want me to tell Coach Rivera?" The reply came fast. "yeah. I can't make it stop." Javier emailed Coach Rivera that night with screenshots. At 10 p.m. the coach posted in the chat: "Clip comes down now. We win and lose as a team. Meeting tomorrow at 7."

qa.q: Who started the pile-on in the chat?
What was Javier feeling as he read the chat?
qa.a: Javier felt uneasy and afraid, with a tight stomach, not brave enough to challenge the captain in public.

qa.q: What was the courageous choice Javier made, and why did it help?
qa.a: He messaged Jamal privately and, with Jamal's okay, sent screenshots to Coach Rivera, so an adult stopped the pile-on that night.

qa.q: How might Jamal see Javier's private message?
qa.a: Jamal probably feels relieved and less alone, since he couldn't make the chat stop by himself.

grounding: Shows a teen who cannot face a public pile-on still messaging the target privately and bringing in the coach.
